Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Vignette:
Kwame Mensah was 78 when he came for treatment, a soft-spoken African immigrant living in the United States, a librarian who had spent years building a life around order, quiet, and predictability. He had been married for decades, and much of his daily routine still revolved around the public library where he worked part-time, shelving returns, helping patrons find books, and keeping watch over the reading room. The event he returned to again and again had happened several years earlier, during what should have been an ordinary community outing in the city. He had gone into a busy public square on a weekend afternoon, a place crowded with families, vendors, and people lingering in the sun. The explosion came without warning. What remained most fixed in his mind was not only the blast itself but the sudden rupture of ordinary human conduct around him: the screaming, the shoving, the desperate pushing past the injured, the sight of people knocking others aside to save themselves. Even now, when he spoke of it, what struck him most was how quickly the world had become lawless and cruel. He had come to believe that when people stopped behaving decently, catastrophe was always close at hand.

In the immediate aftermath, Kwame found that the memory did not settle into the past. It stayed sharp, almost unnervingly complete. He could describe the angle of the afternoon light, the sound of metal striking pavement, the expressions on strangers’ faces, the smell in the air after the blast. He said the memory did not feel like remembering so much as re-entering. It played in his mind like a film he had not chosen to watch, beginning with an ordinary street scene and ending in confusion and terror. Sometimes there was no warning. A moment in the present would simply give way, and the whole scene would be there again in full detail. Over time he noticed that certain situations were especially potent. If he saw people behaving badly in public—someone cutting in line at the library desk, an argument breaking out near the computers, a teenager laughing while another patron complained—his chest tightened and his attention narrowed. In those moments he was no longer only seeing discourtesy; he was bracing for something worse, certain that disorder could turn dangerous in an instant.

Anniversaries of the attack were particularly hard. As the date approached each year, he became more vigilant and withdrawn, tracking the calendar with dread even when he tried not to. News coverage and public conversations about terrorism or mass violence could also pull him back immediately. At the library, patrons often discussed current events near the periodicals section, and if he overheard certain topics—bombings overseas, domestic attacks, public safety failures—he felt the old scene surge forward before he could prepare himself. His responses gradually shaped the way he lived. He stopped going with his wife to festivals, shopping centers, and church events when attendance would be high, insisting that crowded places were too much trouble now. He began turning down invitations that might have brought pleasure—a family cookout, a grandchild’s recital, a neighbor’s retirement party—because he had grown wary of anything that might ask him to relax or feel hopeful. He described this less as sadness than as caution; good moments felt precarious, as though letting his guard down would leave him exposed.

When family gatherings became lively, he sometimes went quiet and seemed to disappear into himself, drifting into an internal world so completely that his wife would have to repeat his name to bring him back. He knew this happened, and he was embarrassed by it, but he also felt that slipping away mentally was easier than staying present when conversation or atmosphere became too charged. At work these patterns had become harder to hide. The library had once suited him perfectly, but now even there he was alert to disruptions. If patrons argued, if a group gathered noisily near the entrance, or if someone began discussing a recent attack on the news, he found himself frozen for a moment, the past arriving all at once with cinematic clarity. He had started arranging his shifts to avoid busier hours and spending more time in back rooms away from the public floor. Colleagues noticed that he no longer joined celebratory staff lunches or retirement gatherings, and his wife had grown hurt by how often he declined outings she hoped they would still share in old age.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was tired of how narrow his life had become. The most recent anniversary had been especially difficult after repeated conversations at the library about a terrorist incident in the news. He found himself replaying his own experience for days, unable to keep the images at a distance, and he realized how little of his world remained outside the event’s reach. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but the sense that any careless remark, any public misbehavior, any crowd could open it again without warning. What he hoped for, carefully and without much flourish, was to be able to stand in the world with his wife, go to work, hear people talk, and not feel that the film might start at any moment.
